questions.lo: The order of metals and carbon in the reactivity series
questions.q: In the reactivity series, where is carbon placed?
options: Below gold, at the bottom
Between aluminium and zinc
Above potassium, at the top
Between iron and copper
questions.explain: Yes. Carbon sits below aluminium and above zinc. Potassium to aluminium are more reactive than carbon; zinc to gold are less reactive.
optionWhy: You may have thought carbon goes after all the metals because it is a non-metal. In fact carbon sits among them, below aluminium and above zinc.
Yes. Carbon sits below aluminium and above zinc. Potassium to aluminium are more reactive than carbon; zinc to gold are less reactive.
You may have thought carbon can take oxygen from any metal, so it must be at the top. In fact carbon is less reactive than potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium and aluminium.
You may have thought carbon marks the point where metals stop reacting with acid. In fact zinc and iron are below carbon and still react; carbon sits between aluminium and zinc.

questions.lo: The order of metals and carbon in the reactivity series
questions.q: A piece of zinc and a piece of copper are put into separate test tubes of dilute hydrochloric acid. What would you see?
options: Only the zinc gives bubbles
Only the copper gives bubbles
Both metals give bubbles
No bubbles on either metal
questions.explain: Yes. Zinc is above copper in the reactivity series and reacts with the acid, so it fizzes. Copper is too unreactive to react with dilute acid.
optionWhy: Yes. Zinc is above copper in the reactivity series and reacts with the acid, so it fizzes. Copper is too unreactive to react with dilute acid.
You may have thought copper is more reactive because copper roofs and statues slowly turn green. In fact zinc is higher in the series: zinc fizzes and copper does not.
You may have thought an acid eats away any metal. In fact copper is too low in the series to react with dilute acid, so only the zinc fizzes.
You may have thought the metals below carbon do not react at all. In fact zinc still reacts with dilute acid and fizzes; copper does not.

questions.lo: The order of metals and carbon in the reactivity series
questions.q: Which statement about the reactivity series is correct?
options: Iron is more reactive than sodium
Iron is more reactive than aluminium
Calcium is more reactive than iron
Copper is more reactive than carbon
questions.explain: Yes. Calcium is near the top of the series, above carbon, while iron is below carbon, so calcium is much more reactive.
optionWhy: You may have thought iron is more reactive because it is hard and strong, while sodium is soft. In fact reactivity is not hardness: sodium is near the top of the series.
You may have thought aluminium is unreactive because it does not rust. In fact aluminium is above iron; a thin oxide coat on its surface protects it.
Yes. Calcium is near the top of the series, above carbon, while iron is below carbon, so calcium is much more reactive.
You may have thought carbon goes below all the metals because it is a non-metal. In fact carbon is above copper, which is why carbon can take oxygen from copper oxide.

questions.lo: The order of metals and carbon in the reactivity series
questions.q: Magnesium reacts very slowly with cold water. Which element reacts faster than magnesium with cold water?
options: Iron (Fe)
Carbon (C)
Copper (Cu)
Calcium (Ca)
questions.explain: Yes. Calcium is above magnesium in the reactivity series, so it reacts faster: it bubbles steadily in cold water.
optionWhy: You may have thought iron is more reactive because it is a hard, strong metal. In fact iron is below magnesium in the series and gives no bubbles in cold water.
You may have thought carbon is above every metal because it extracts metals. In fact carbon is below magnesium and does not react with cold water.

You may have thought copper reacts with water because copper roofs turn green in the rain. In fact that green coat forms over many years; copper is near the bottom of the series and does not react with cold water.
Yes. Calcium is above magnesium in the reactivity series, so it reacts faster: it bubbles steadily in cold water.

questions.lo: The use of carbon in obtaining metals from metal oxides
questions.q: Copper oxide powder is heated strongly with carbon powder. What does the carbon do?
options: It takes the oxygen from the copper oxide
It burns to make heat that frees the copper
It joins on to the copper to make a compound
It destroys all the oxygen in the copper oxide
questions.explain: Yes. Carbon is more reactive than copper, so it takes the oxygen and becomes carbon dioxide: copper oxide + carbon → copper + carbon dioxide.
optionWhy: Yes. Carbon is more reactive than copper, so it takes the oxygen and becomes carbon dioxide: copper oxide + carbon → copper + carbon dioxide.
You may have thought carbon is only a fuel. In fact heating copper oxide on its own does not give copper; the carbon reacts and takes the oxygen.
You may have thought the carbon combines with the copper. In fact the carbon joins with the oxygen, leaving copper on its own.
You may have thought the oxygen disappears. In fact no oxygen is destroyed: it joins with carbon to make carbon dioxide gas, which you cannot see.

questions.lo: The use of carbon in obtaining metals from metal oxides
questions.q: In a furnace, iron oxide is heated strongly with carbon. What are the products?
options: Iron carbonate alone
Iron and oxygen gas
Iron and nothing else
Iron and carbon dioxide
questions.explain: Yes. Carbon takes the oxygen from the iron oxide: iron oxide + carbon → iron + carbon dioxide.
optionWhy: You may have thought the carbon joins the iron to make a carbonate. In fact the carbon joins with the oxygen, so iron is left on its own and carbon dioxide forms.
You may have thought the heat splits iron oxide into iron and oxygen. In fact the oxygen leaves joined to carbon, as carbon dioxide.
You may have thought the oxygen and carbon are burnt away. In fact no atoms are destroyed: they leave together as carbon dioxide gas.
Yes. Carbon takes the oxygen from the iron oxide: iron oxide + carbon → iron + carbon dioxide.

questions.lo: The use of carbon in obtaining metals from metal oxides
questions.q: Lead is less reactive than iron but more reactive than copper. Which statement about getting lead from lead oxide is correct?
options: Carbon can extract it, as carbon extracts any metal
Carbon can extract it, as lead is below carbon
Carbon cannot extract it, as carbon is below lead
Carbon cannot extract it, as lead is unreactive
questions.explain: Yes. Lead is below iron, so it is below carbon too. Carbon is more reactive, so it takes the oxygen: lead oxide + carbon → lead + carbon dioxide.
optionWhy: You may have thought carbon works for every metal. Carbon does extract lead, but only because lead is below carbon; it cannot extract metals above it, such as aluminium.
Yes. Lead is below iron, so it is below carbon too. Carbon is more reactive, so it takes the oxygen: lead oxide + carbon → lead + carbon dioxide.
You may have thought carbon goes below all the metals because it is a non-metal. In fact carbon is above zinc and iron, so it is above lead too and can take lead oxide's oxygen.
You may have thought less reactive metals are harder to extract. In fact it is the other way round: lead is below carbon, so carbon can take its oxygen.

questions.lo: The use of carbon in obtaining metals from metal oxides
questions.q: Zinc oxide is heated with carbon, and the zinc oxide is reduced. In chemistry, what does 'reduced' mean?
options: It has gained oxygen
It has become smaller
It has lost its oxygen
It has joined to carbon
questions.explain: Yes. At KS3, reduction is loss of oxygen. Carbon takes the oxygen, so zinc is left.
optionWhy: You may have mixed up reduction and oxidation. Gaining oxygen is oxidation; it is the carbon that gains oxygen here.
You may have used the everyday meaning of 'reduced'. In chemistry it means losing oxygen; the solid does get lighter, but only because its oxygen has gone.
Yes. At KS3, reduction is loss of oxygen. Carbon takes the oxygen, so zinc is left.
You may have thought the carbon joins on to the zinc. In fact the carbon joins the oxygen and leaves as carbon dioxide.

questions.lo: The use of carbon in obtaining metals from metal oxides
questions.q: The diagram shows part of the reactivity series, with a new metal, X. How would metal X most likely be obtained?
options: By heating X oxide with carbon
By heating X oxide on its own
By digging up pure X from rocks
By electrolysis of a compound of X
questions.explain: Yes. X is above carbon, so carbon cannot take the oxygen from X oxide. Metals above carbon are extracted another way, such as electrolysis.
optionWhy: You may have thought carbon can extract any metal. In fact X is above carbon in the diagram, so carbon cannot take its oxygen.
You may have thought heat alone frees a metal from its oxide. In fact heating the oxide of a metal as reactive as X does not remove the oxygen; X is too reactive even for carbon.
You may have thought metals are found as the pure metal. In fact a metal as reactive as X is always found joined to other elements in compounds.
Yes. X is above carbon, so carbon cannot take the oxygen from X oxide. Metals above carbon are extracted another way, such as electrolysis.

questions.lo: The use of carbon in obtaining metals from metal oxides
questions.q: In a furnace, zinc oxide and aluminium oxide are each heated strongly with carbon. Which metal is made?
options: Zinc, but not aluminium
Aluminium, but not zinc
Both zinc and aluminium
Neither of these metals
questions.explain: Yes. Zinc is below carbon, so carbon takes the oxygen from zinc oxide. Aluminium is above carbon, so carbon cannot take its oxygen.
optionWhy: Yes. Zinc is below carbon, so carbon takes the oxygen from zinc oxide. Aluminium is above carbon, so carbon cannot take its oxygen.
You may have thought a more reactive metal is easier to extract. In fact it is harder: carbon cannot take oxygen from aluminium oxide.
You may have thought carbon can extract any metal. In fact carbon only works for metals below it, so aluminium is not made.
You may have thought carbon is below all the metals. In fact carbon is above zinc, so it can take the oxygen from zinc oxide.

questions.lo: Properties of ceramics, polymers and composites (qualitative)
questions.q: Which statement about materials is correct?
options: Metals are very good heat insulators
A kettle case is too hard to be a polymer
Ceramics are hard but can shatter
Carbon fibre is light and so it is weak
questions.explain: Yes. Ceramics are hard and stiff, but they are brittle, so a mug or tile can crack or shatter when dropped.
optionWhy: You may have thought metal flasks keep drinks hot because metal insulates. In fact metals are good heat conductors; the flask works because of a vacuum.
You may have thought all plastics are soft and bendy. In fact some polymers are hard and stiff: kettle cases and plugs are made of them.
Yes. Ceramics are hard and stiff, but they are brittle, so a mug or tile can crack or shatter when dropped.
You may have thought light materials must be weak. In fact carbon fibre is light but strong, which is why it is used for bike frames.

questions.lo: Properties of ceramics, polymers and composites (qualitative)
questions.q: Which of these statements is correct?
options: Tiles are so hard that they do not crack
Plastic bottles soften when heated
Foam insulates, so it stays solid in a fire
Fibreglass shatters just like glass
questions.explain: Yes. Plastic bottles are made of a polymer, and most polymers soften or melt when heated. That is why plastic is not used for very hot jobs.
optionWhy: You may have thought very hard means hard to break. In fact ceramic tiles are hard but brittle, so they can crack or shatter when something hits them.
Yes. Plastic bottles are made of a polymer, and most polymers soften or melt when heated. That is why plastic is not used for very hot jobs.
You may have thought a heat insulator must stand great heat. In fact polystyrene foam is a good insulator but melts and burns at quite low temperatures.
You may have thought a composite keeps the properties of each part. In fact the plastic holds the glass fibres, so fibreglass does not shatter like glass.

questions.lo: Properties of ceramics, polymers and composites (qualitative)
questions.q: A kiln heats pottery to over 1000 °C. Which material is best for lining the inside of the kiln?
options: A ceramic, as it stays solid when very hot
A polymer, as it is a good heat insulator
A metal, as it is a good heat insulator
Fibreglass, as it has the properties of glass
questions.explain: Yes. Ceramics stay solid at very high temperatures and let heat through only slowly, so they are used to line kilns and furnaces.
optionWhy: Yes. Ceramics stay solid at very high temperatures and let heat through only slowly, so they are used to line kilns and furnaces.
You may have thought a good insulator can stand great heat. In fact polymers soften, melt or burn far below 1000 °C.
You may have thought metals insulate. In fact metals are good heat conductors, so a metal lining would let heat escape.
You may have thought a composite has every property of its parts. In fact the plastic in fibreglass would soften and burn at kiln temperatures.

questions.lo: Properties of ceramics, polymers and composites (qualitative)
questions.q: The diagram shows fibreglass: thin glass fibres held in a plastic. Compared with a sheet of glass, fibreglass is …
options: weaker, because it is lighter than glass
just as soft and bendy as plastic
better for hot jobs as it insulates
much less likely to shatter when hit
questions.explain: Yes. The plastic holds the fibres and stops cracks spreading, so fibreglass is tough, while a glass sheet is brittle.
optionWhy: You may have thought a lighter material must be weaker. In fact fibreglass is light and strong; that is why boats are made of it.
You may have thought anything containing plastic is soft and bendy. In fact the glass fibres make fibreglass stiff and strong.
You may have thought a heat insulator can stand great heat. In fact the plastic in fibreglass softens at temperatures that glass can stand.
Yes. The plastic holds the fibres and stops cracks spreading, so fibreglass is tough, while a glass sheet is brittle.

questions.lo: Properties of ceramics, polymers and composites (qualitative)
questions.q: The diagram shows reinforced concrete: steel rods inside concrete. Concrete on its own cracks easily when it is bent. What do the steel rods do?
options: Nothing, as it is just a mixture
They stop it snapping when it bends
They make it so hard it cannot crack
They keep heat out, as metals insulate
questions.explain: Yes. Concrete is strong when squashed but cracks when bent; the steel rods hold it together, so the composite does not snap.
optionWhy: You may have thought the parts just keep their own properties. In fact the rods and concrete work together, giving a material that resists bending.
Yes. Concrete is strong when squashed but cracks when bent; the steel rods hold it together, so the composite does not snap.
You may have thought hardness stops cracking. In fact the rods do not make the concrete harder; they stop it snapping when bent.
You may have thought metals are heat insulators. In fact metals conduct heat well; the rods are there to stop the concrete snapping.
